lesson.title: When Current Falls Behind: Lagging Power Factor and Inductive Loads
lesson.summary: A lagging power factor describes the common situation where current in an AC circuit trails voltage in phase because of inductive reactance, a signature of motors, transformers, and other winding-based loads.
lesson.body:
Power factor is the ratio of real power to apparent power, cos(theta), but that number alone does not say everything: a power factor of 0.6 could describe two very different circuits, one where current trails behind voltage and one where it runs ahead. The word lagging specifies the first case: the current phasor sits behind the voltage phasor by angle theta, reaching its peak, zero crossing, and trough each a little later in time than voltage does. This is the everyday situation for inductive loads. An inductor resists any change in the current through it, generating a back electromotive force that delays how quickly current can build up in response to an applied voltage, so on a phasor diagram the current arrow trails the voltage arrow as both sweep around together.

Because this lag comes from inductive reactance, its size tracks XL = wL directly: a larger inductance, or a higher operating frequency, means a larger XL relative to R, a bigger phase angle theta, and a lower, more lagging power factor. This matters practically because most heavy industrial and commercial loads, induction motors, transformers, fluorescent and older ballasts, are fundamentally coils of wire and are inherently inductive. Lagging power factor is therefore the default condition utilities plan around, which is exactly why power factor correction, discussed with the power triangle, almost always means adding capacitors, which push current the opposite way, leading, rather than adding more inductance.

Model an induction motor as a series R and XL combination, R = 6 ohms and XL = 8 ohms, fed by a 240 V RMS supply. The impedance is Z = 6 + j8 ohms, with magnitude |Z| = sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt(36 + 64) = sqrt(100) = 10 ohms and angle theta = arctan(8/6) = 53.13 degrees. The current is I = V/Z = 240/10 = 24 A, lagging the voltage by 53.13 degrees, a lagging power factor of cos(53.13 degrees) = 0.6. The apparent power is S = VI = 240 times 24 = 5760 VA. Using sin(53.13 degrees) = 0.8, the real power is P = S cos(theta) = 5760 times 0.6 = 3456 W and the reactive power is Q = S sin(theta) = 5760 times 0.8 = 4608 VAR.

Check the arithmetic with the power triangle relationship, P^2 + Q^2 = S^2: 3456^2 + 4608^2 = 11,943,936 + 21,233,664 = 33,177,600, and 5760^2 = 33,177,600 as well, confirming the numbers are self-consistent. This motor draws 24 A to deliver only 3456 W of useful mechanical output, with the remaining 4608 VAR shuttling in and out of its windings every cycle. Utilities describe this precisely as 0.6 lagging rather than just 0.6, because the direction of the phase shift determines the fix: a lagging load needs capacitive VARs added to pull its power factor back toward 1, while a leading load, less common in practice, would need the opposite treatment entirely, adding inductance rather than capacitance to bring the angle back toward zero.
